newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish finance minister eyes leaner 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: Polish finance minister eyes leaner 1998 budget.

text.p: Poland should have a leaner, tighter budget for 1998 which will take into account planned tax cuts, caps on deficit financing and lower privatisation revenues, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday.

Belka told Reuters in an interview the 1998 draft, which his ministry had already started preparing, would be based on the assumption that a new constitution, now debated in parliament, would bar government financing in the central bank.
"We should expect a real drop in revenues and spending in relation to GDP and a lower deficit and therefore spending should focus on a few key areas," Belka said.
The 1997 budget assumes a deficit of 2.8 percent of GDP with growth seen at about 5.5 percent and inflation targeted to fall to 13 percent from 18.5 percent in December 1996.
Belka said it was still to early to give any specific targets for next year but said the budget plan would aim to achieve single-digit inflation while maintaining the current rate of growth.

He said inflation data for the first quarter of this year was optimistic with year-on-year inflation seen falling to or just below 17 percent in March and allowed to set ambitious goals for next year.
He said the scope of the budget would be limited by the planned cut in personal and corporate income taxes and plans to use privatisation revenues for such programmes as social security reform.
Late last year the parliament passed a one point reduction in personal income taxes and also obliged the next parliament and govenrment to further cut taxes in 1998.
Belka also said that 1997 budget would probably be the last to draw significant funds from privatisation.

"Even though we will be privatising some very important firms in 1998 we will will want to use a large portion of privatisation revenues on such social programmes as supporting the social security reform," he said.

He said that even such a tight budget would allow to increase real spending on some key areas if the government concentrates on only a few priorities and economic growth continues at the current rate.
The budget draft, prepared by the finance ministry will be debated and eventually implemented by a new parliament and cabinet after parliamentary polls due in the fourth quarter.

Public opinion polls show an alliance of right-wing parties led by the Solidarity trade union stands a chance of winning the vote and ending the four-year rule of the coalition of the ex-comunist Democratic Left Alliance and the Peasant Party.
But asked whether the election could result in a radical shift in economic policy Belka said:
"I cannot imagine any political force producing a finance minister who unlike my predecessors and myself would not fight for sound national finances."

Belka, an economics professor, who replaced another academic Grzegorz Kolodko last month after serving for more than a year as economic adviser to President Aleksander Kwasniewski, said he also expected the election campaign to have a limited impact on Poland's economy.
"Strikes and social unrests are likely to occur but I believe it won't change the macroeconomic picture it can affect particular firms but not the whole country."
"For example I don't see that anyone would fear to privatise companies because of the upcoming elections."
